Day 14 of 100 · AWS Networking Foundations

Review + Practical Lab

Day 14 consolidated the first networking concepts into a practical lab so identity, addressing, routing and filtering were tested as one path rather than memorized separately.

Architecture / mental model

VPC → public/private subnets → route tables → IGW/NAT/endpoints → Security Groups/NACLs → EC2 test workloads

How it works

A review lab should force each earlier component to justify its place: IAM controls who can change the environment; the VPC and subnets define address/placement boundaries; route tables choose paths; gateways/endpoints provide connectivity; Security Groups and NACLs filter traffic.

The useful exercise is not merely creating each resource. It is predicting a request path before testing it, then changing one control and explaining exactly why the result changes.

A practical lab also exposes hidden dependencies. A private EC2 instance that cannot reach a package repository may have a NAT-route problem, while a public instance that times out on SSH may be blocked at Security Group, NACL, route, addressing or host level.

Hands-on reference

aws ec2 describe-vpcs
aws ec2 describe-subnets
aws ec2 describe-route-tables
aws ec2 describe-security-groups
aws ec2 describe-network-acls
aws ec2 describe-internet-gateways
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways

Verification

Draw one end-to-end path for public inbound access and one for private outbound access, then prove each layer with AWS API output and an application-level test.

Field note / gotcha

A lab that only proves resources exist is inventory, not networking verification. The packet path is the evidence.

Security considerations

Tear down temporary resources after the lab, remove broad test rules and confirm no test instance, Elastic IP, NAT Gateway or load balancer remains billable/exposed.

What I learned

Review becomes useful when the concepts collide in one system and failures can be traced instead of guessed.
